compute: Apple M-series laptop (arm64), no GPU, no Docker; two days of wall clock
backend: api.deepseek.com, model `deepseek-flash` (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), OpenAI-compatible, token logprobs available
wallclock: ≈80 min of verifier time in total: 30 min for the two configurations on seed 0, ≈50 min for seeds 1 and 2
deviation_note: Verifier model, seed count and task scope differ from the paper; tasks, metric and evaluation code are the authors' own.
mod_note: Each configuration writes its own score cache; no verifier score is shared between baseline and ablation.
mod_finding: Coarsening the scale from 20 letters to 5 leaves task-level selection unchanged, and this now holds under repetition: the baseline selects a successful rollout on 11 of 12 tasks in all three seeds (91.7% ± 0.0), and the ablation repeats that 11 of 12 on the shared seed. The finer statistics show the seed noise the task counting is too coarse to resolve — pairwise preference accuracy is 90.3 / 88.6 / 93.9 across seeds (90.9 ± 2.7) and trial AUC is 0.861 / 0.843 / 0.818 (0.841 ± 0.022) — while the g5 run, on the same 282 of 288 comparisons, lands within that band (90.6% pairwise, 0.852 AUC). At vote level the ablation does move things: 21/186 informative comparisons flip (11.3%) against 29/96 uninformative ones (30.2%), and the margin widens from 0.317 to 0.369. Because a task decision aggregates 30 votes, those flips cancel. The honest claim is 'no difference larger than about two tasks', which is what a one-hot score distribution predicts.
